paragraphs: The paper combines two ways of representing text: neural sequence modeling, which captures how words unfold, and topic modeling, which captures the themes connecting a document. Its model explicitly assigns a discrete topic variable to each word. These assignments make thematic structure part of the model rather than leaving it entirely implicit in a neural representation.

The central contribution concerns how to train this combination. The authors use neural variational inference without relying on stochastic backpropagation to handle the discrete variables. This matters because the model retains explicit word-level topic choices while benefiting from neural methods for representing text sequences. The approach brings local sequence information and global thematic coherence into the same learning framework.

Across multiple corpora, the authors report improved perplexity and document understanding. They also study how prior parameters affect both the model and its variational parameters. On an automatic topic-quality measure, the approach can match and surpass a popular topic-model implementation. Together, these findings support the usefulness of the proposed combination for both text prediction and thematic representation.
neurips-2020-a-discrete-variational-recu.tldr: A neural topic model learns explicit word-level topic assignments without stochastic backpropagation through discrete variables, improving reported text and topic-quality results.

paragraphs: Distributional reinforcement learning represents the range of possible long-term outcomes instead of only their average. The paper starts from evidence suggesting that dopamine systems may perform this kind of learning. A difficulty with previously explored representations is that computing a unit's prediction error requires information about other units, making the required computation difficult to explain in realistic neural circuits.

The authors introduce the Laplace code, which separates reward information along three dimensions: reward magnitude, temporal discounting, and time horizon. These connect respectively to distributional quantiles, the Laplace transform of future rewards, and eligibility traces. The separation supports a local temporal-difference learning rule while retaining a rich representation of possible outcomes.

The representation also recovers how the immediate reward distribution evolves over future time, rather than only summarizing long-run value. This gives it the capacity to represent which rewards may occur at different future moments. The resulting computations can immediately adjust to changed horizons or discount factors. The contribution is a computationally straightforward candidate code with these capabilities, rather than a demonstration that biological circuits necessarily use it.
neurips-2020-a-local-temporal-difference.tldr: The Laplace code supports local distributional reinforcement learning while representing possible rewards across future times and adapting to changed horizons or discounting.

paragraphs: Random Fourier feature regression is often understood through its connection to a limiting Gaussian kernel as the number of features grows. This paper studies a different regime: the sample count, input dimension, and feature count all grow together and remain comparable. That distinction matters because the familiar kernel limit no longer describes the random feature Gram matrix in this setting.

The authors use random matrix analysis to characterize the exact asymptotic behavior that replaces that limit. Their results provide accurate estimates of training and test regression errors when all three dimensions are large. The analysis therefore connects the relative sizes of the data and feature representation to prediction performance, rather than treating the feature count as independently approaching infinity.

From these error estimates, the paper identifies two qualitatively different learning phases and precisely describes the transition between them. It derives the associated double-descent test-error curve from that transition. The results do not require strong assumptions about the data distribution, and the authors report close agreement with experiments on real-world datasets. The stated theory concerns this joint large-dimension regime.
neurips-2020-a-random-matrix-analysis-of.tldr: A joint large-dimension analysis of random Fourier feature regression explains its learning phase transition and resulting double-descent test error.

paragraphs: Two decision makers can achieve similar accuracy while succeeding and failing on different inputs. The paper argues that aggregate accuracy therefore cannot establish whether they use similar strategies, especially when both perform very well. It introduces trial-by-trial error consistency to measure whether their mistakes systematically occur on the same examples.

The analysis can compare humans with humans, algorithms with algorithms, or humans with algorithms. Consistent errors are treated as a necessary condition for establishing similar processing strategies, not as sufficient proof of a shared strategy. Looking at the locations of errors adds information that a single overall success rate hides.

In visual object recognition, the tested convolutional networks show strong consistency with one another across architectures. Their consistency with humans is only slightly above chance, suggesting substantially different strategies. The recurrent model CORnet-S also misses essential characteristics of human behavior and resembles a feedforward ResNet-50 in this analysis. Thus, the observed behavioral mismatch extends beyond feedforward models. Error consistency provides a way to assess whether future systems move closer to human patterns of decisions.
neurips-2020-beyond-accuracy-quantifying.tldr: Comparing which images cause errors reveals substantial behavioral differences between humans and tested vision networks that overall accuracy can conceal.

paragraphs: CaSPR represents objects that move or change shape using sequences of point clouds. Its goal is to combine observations over time and support queries about an object's past state, including locations and times that were not directly observed. This requires a representation that remains meaningful when measurements arrive irregularly or contain different numbers of points.

The method first maps a point-cloud sequence into a canonical object space that explicitly includes time. This creates a common representation for observations across the sequence. It then uses neural ordinary differential equations to learn a continuous spatiotemporal latent representation, together with continuous normalizing flows to model evolving shapes generatively.

The authors report representations that support continuity across space and time, tolerate irregular sampling, and generalize to unseen object instances. They demonstrate the approach through shape reconstruction, camera pose estimation, continuous sequence reconstruction, and correspondence estimation. These applications show why bringing observations into a shared object-centered representation matters: the model can aggregate incomplete measurements and use their temporal relationships to infer object structure across a sequence.
neurips-2020-caspr-learning-canonical-sp.tldr: CaSPR learns continuous object-centered representations of changing point clouds to combine irregular observations and reconstruct object states across space and time.

paragraphs: Compressed sensing with a generative prior seeks a signal from a small number of measurements by restricting reconstruction to outputs of a neural generator. Existing theory supports efficient approximate recovery from noisy measurements for signals in the range of networks with random Gaussian weights. However, those guarantees required every layer to grow over the previous one by a logarithmic factor.

The paper weakens this expansion requirement to a constant factor, showing that constant expansion suffices for efficient recovery and is also information-theoretically necessary in the studied setting. This makes the architectural growth required by the theory substantially less demanding. The result retains the stated generative-network setting rather than establishing recovery for arbitrary generators.

The proof introduces a uniform concentration theorem for random functions satisfying a relaxed smoothness property called pseudo-Lipschitzness. It uses that theorem to establish the Weight Distribution Condition for Gaussian matrices with constant aspect ratios. Because this condition underpins existing recovery guarantees, the improvement carries over to related results, including one-bit recovery and phase retrieval. The contribution is therefore both a sharper recovery guarantee and a reusable theoretical tool.
neurips-2020-constant-expansion-suffices.tldr: For the studied Gaussian-weight generators, constant layer expansion suffices for efficient compressed-sensing recovery, weakening a previous logarithmic expansion requirement.

paragraphs: Predicting a video far into the future requires learning relationships that extend across both space and time. The paper addresses this challenge with a higher-order convolutional LSTM that combines information from a history of convolutional features. Its aim is to capture longer-term correlations while keeping the representation of that history compact.

The key component is a tensor-train module that combines features across time for prediction. A direct higher-order model would impose substantial computation and memory demands, so the authors introduce a convolutional tensor-train decomposition. It jointly approximates a sequence of convolutional kernels through a low-rank factorization, reducing the complexity of modeling those temporal relationships.

The authors report stronger performance than existing approaches while using only a fraction of their parameters, including those of baseline models. They report state-of-the-art results for multistep video prediction on Moving-MNIST-2 and KTH, and early activity recognition on Something-Something V2. These findings support the idea that a compact factorization can make richer temporal modeling practical, improving the evaluated tasks without requiring a correspondingly large parameter count.
neurips-2020-convolutional-tensor-train-.tldr: A tensor-train convolutional LSTM captures longer-term video relationships with fewer parameters and reports strong prediction and early-recognition results.

paragraphs: The paper studies policy evaluation by a network of cooperating agents. Each agent observes transitions in a shared environment but has locally private rewards. Together, the agents seek to estimate the policy's value function. Linear function approximation makes this estimation scalable by representing values through a limited collection of features.

The proposed algorithm combines temporal-difference learning with gradient tracking. This produces a decentralized TD tracker that goes beyond the consensus-style approaches discussed in the abstract. The central design issue is how agents can coordinate their learning across the communication graph while working with rewards that are observed locally.

The authors establish finite-time properties through a unified multistep Lyapunov analysis, covering both independent transitions and transitions with Markovian dependence. Their analysis avoids the limiting dependence on the number of agents present in earlier error bounds and yields performance comparable to the sharpest centralized TD results described in the abstract. This is significant because it gives a theoretical account of decentralized evaluation after finite amounts of learning, including when successive observations are dependent.
neurips-2020-decentralized-td-tracking-w.tldr: Combining TD learning with gradient tracking gives decentralized policy evaluation finite-time guarantees comparable to strong centralized results.

paragraphs: Automodulators are generative autoencoders designed both to reconstruct real input images and to combine several inputs into a new image. The combination enables immediate style mixing from arbitrary collections of input images. This brings image fusion into a model that can also reproduce particular observed images.

The decoder separates the flow of data through its operations from the statistical properties used to modulate those operations. A latent vector controls this modulation, and the method includes a principled approach to disentangling decoder layers from one another. Related decoder designs had been explored with generative adversarial networks focused on random sampling; the autoencoder setting connects the mechanism directly to real inputs.

The authors introduce training techniques that produce sharp, high-resolution outputs and demonstrate them on four image datasets. They report state-of-the-art results in autoencoder comparisons and visual quality close to leading GANs. These findings support the model's combination of reconstruction and generation capabilities. Its proposed usefulness in other image applications and data domains is presented as an expectation, while the stated demonstrations concern image datasets and style mixing.
neurips-2020-deep-automodulators-62d6ecf.tldr: Automodulators reconstruct real images and mix their styles through latent-controlled decoder modulation, producing sharp high-resolution outputs.

paragraphs: Many data structures contain other structures: a sequence may contain sets, or a graph may contain smaller graphs. Neural networks can respect the symmetries of individual building blocks, but combining those rules for a hierarchy requires a broader framework. This paper develops such a framework for constructing equivariant maps, whose outputs change consistently with transformations of their inputs.

The authors identify the symmetry of the hierarchy through a mathematical construction called the wreath product. They then express the hierarchical equivariant map as a combination of equivariant linear layers for the component structures. Their characterization shows that maps respecting the hierarchy's symmetry have this form, giving the construction a theoretical basis beyond an architectural recipe.

For an application, the authors voxelize point clouds, organizing the data into a hierarchy with translation and permutation symmetries. They use the resulting model for semantic segmentation and report state-of-the-art results on semantic3d, s3dis, and vkitti. These experiments connect the abstract symmetry framework to practical model design: the organization of the data determines how the network should share and transform information.
neurips-2020-equivariant-networks-for-hi.tldr: A symmetry-based framework builds equivariant networks for hierarchical data and achieves reported state-of-the-art point-cloud segmentation results.

paragraphs: In some allocation problems, an action's result arrives only after a random delay that depends on the chosen action. Hiring for a task and allocating a server are examples in the abstract. Decisions must therefore account for elapsed time, completion deadlines, and how a total time budget is divided among groups.

The paper formulates this setting as continuous-time utility maximization. Different utility choices recover reward maximization, max-min fairness, and proportional fairness as special cases. It characterizes an optimal offline policy that divides time according to the selected fairness objective and uses deadlines to improve time efficiency. Fairness is thus defined through the utility function rather than imposed as one universal allocation rule.

When the relevant statistics are unknown, the authors propose an online algorithm based on dual ascent for time averages. They prove a regret bound of order B to the power of minus one-half, up to logarithmic factors, where B is the total time budget. This connects learning under action-dependent delays with explicit allocation preferences and provides a guarantee that improves as the time budget grows.
neurips-2020-group-fair-online-allocatio.tldr: A continuous-time allocation framework combines action-dependent delays, deadlines, and group fairness with an online algorithm that has a diminishing regret bound.

paragraphs: Repeated neural recordings contain activity tied to a stimulus or behavior and fluctuations that vary between trials. For this analysis, the paper calls the former signal and the latter noise. Separating their shared structure helps distinguish how a neural population represents repeated events from how its activity varies around that representation.

The authors introduce signal-noise Poisson-spiking Gaussian Process Factor Analysis, a latent-variable model that separates these components in population spiking data. A Fourier-domain variational inference method identifies smooth latent structure efficiently. The model is also extended to capture statistical relationships between different brain regions, allowing the analysis to ask whether fluctuations are shared across regions.

In monkey V1 recordings, the model finds noise fluctuations in a subspace orthogonal to signal activity. This suggests that trial-level fluctuations need not interfere with the represented signal in those data. In mouse visual cortex, models with noise shared across regions outperform models assigning independent noise to each region. Together, the findings show how separating signal and noise structure can reveal both their geometric relationship within a population and their statistical relationships across regions.
neurips-2020-identifying-signal-and-nois.tldr: A Gaussian process factor model separates stimulus-linked neural activity from trial fluctuations and reveals distinct signal geometry and shared noise across regions.

paragraphs: Speech carries information over multiple timescales, and brain-response models can use language-model representations to predict fMRI activity. However, ordinary language-model features mix these timescales together. That makes it difficult to interpret a prediction in terms of how much temporal context a particular brain location represents.

The authors construct an LSTM language model whose individual units are forced to integrate information over specified temporal scales. This makes the timescale associated with a feature explicit and supports direct mapping of timescale information to individual fMRI voxels. They also modify the fMRI encoding procedure to account for differences in the temporal properties of the features, so that both short- and long-timescale information can be captured.

The resulting approach outperforms other encoding models, with particular gains for voxels representing long-timescale information. It also provides a more detailed map of timescale information along the human language pathway. The contribution links interpretability and prediction: controlling how language-model units accumulate context makes their relationship to measured brain responses easier to examine, while the revised encoding procedure improves the reported predictions.
neurips-2020-interpretable-multi-timesca.tldr: Explicitly controlling language-model timescales improves fMRI prediction and helps map how brain locations represent speech over different temporal spans.

paragraphs: Risk-sensitive learning chooses a model according to preferences about the distribution of losses, rather than simply their average. The paper studies how well such choices generalize from training data. It uses optimized certainty equivalents, or OCEs, as a common framework encompassing risks such as entropic risk, mean-variance objectives, and conditional value-at-risk.

The authors give two guarantees for a hypothesis that minimizes empirical OCE. The first directly bounds its OCE performance using the Rademacher average of the hypothesis space, a measure of that space's complexity. This extends and improves existing results for expected loss and conditional value-at-risk, connecting multiple risk objectives through one analysis.

The second guarantee concerns expected loss even though training optimizes a risk-sensitive objective. It uses a new variance-based characterization of OCE and reduces dependence on the chosen OCE's smoothness. The two bounds therefore address different questions: performance under the selected risk criterion and performance under average loss. Exploratory neural-network experiments illustrate practical implications of the theory, while the central contribution is the generalization analysis across these risk-sensitive learning schemes.
neurips-2020-learning-bounds-for-risk-se.tldr: A unified analysis gives risk-sensitive learners guarantees for both their chosen risk objective and expected loss.

paragraphs: Operator-valued kernels support supervised learning where both inputs and outputs can be functions. Efficient approaches have relied heavily on positive definiteness, a mathematical property that can restrict which kernels are usable. This paper investigates how to learn with operator-valued kernels that may lack that property.

The authors use reproducing kernel Krein spaces of function-valued functions to accommodate indefinite kernels. They present a representer theorem that leads to a suitable loss-stabilization problem. This supplies a mathematical route from the broader kernel setting to a concrete learning formulation, rather than requiring the kernel to satisfy the usual positive-definiteness assumption.

The paper also analyzes generalization and proposes an iterative solver called Operator based Minimum Residual, or OpMINRES, for the stabilization problem. Experiments with synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the utility of learning with indefinite operator-valued kernels. The contribution combines a function-space formulation, learning analysis, and an optimization algorithm, widening the kernel choices available for functional input-output problems. The empirical claim is that this approach is useful in the evaluated settings, rather than that indefiniteness itself always improves prediction.
neurips-2020-learning-with-operator-valu.tldr: A Krein-space framework and iterative solver enable supervised learning with operator-valued kernels that need not be positive definite.

paragraphs: Random features make kernel learning more scalable, but the choice of sampling distribution matters. A distribution optimized for the data can reduce the number of features needed to reach a desired accuracy. The obstacle addressed here is the computational difficulty of drawing features from that optimized distribution.

The authors develop a quantum sampling algorithm with runtime linear in the input dimension D. For this sampling task, they report an exponential speedup in D over every known classical algorithm. The comparison is specifically to known classical methods, and the stated advantage concerns optimized feature sampling. The algorithm also avoids the sparsity and low-rank assumptions used by existing quantum learning approaches discussed in the abstract.

The paper then connects the sampling procedure to regression trained with stochastic gradient descent. It shows that this downstream learning stage can be performed without eliminating the exponential speedup. That connection matters because a faster sampling subroutine is useful for learning only if later computation preserves its benefit. The result is a quantum-assisted learning framework built around data-adapted random features.
neurips-2020-learning-with-optimized-ran.tldr: A quantum algorithm samples optimized random features in linear input dimension, exponentially faster than known classical samplers, with a regression stage that preserves the advantage.

paragraphs: The paper studies optimization problems that can be expressed through competing minimization and maximization steps. Optimal transport is one member of the class, but the aim is broader: to place a range of related problems in a shared MinMax framework. This makes it possible to investigate common mathematical and computational tools across them.

A central focus is regularization. The authors extend techniques from classical optimal transport and prove approximation results that justify solving the regularized problems with neural networks. They also illustrate fundamental problems that arise without regularization. Regularization therefore plays a role in establishing why neural-network approximations are appropriate for the optimization problems under study.

The paper connects this framework to generative adversarial networks and examines which algorithmic techniques from that literature suit the studied problems. Numerical experiments demonstrate the breadth of the framework and investigate which theoretical insights are most helpful in practice. The overall contribution joins formulation, approximation theory, and numerical methods, showing how a common MinMax viewpoint can guide neural-network solutions across optimal transport and related settings.
neurips-2020-minmax-methods-for-optimal-.tldr: A shared MinMax framework uses regularization and approximation theory to support neural-network solutions for optimal transport and related problems.

paragraphs: In multi-agent active perception, a team gathers observations to estimate something hidden. Agents act separately, but their observations are combined only after the task ends. This creates a planning difficulty: the quality of the final estimate is judged centrally, even though the information-gathering decisions are decentralized.

The authors model the task as a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process with a convex centralized prediction reward. They introduce an individual prediction action for each agent, converting the problem into a standard form with decentralized prediction rewards. They bound the loss introduced by decentralization and give a sufficient condition under which that loss is zero. The condition guarantees zero loss when it holds; it is not presented as necessary.

This conversion makes standard Dec-POMDP solution algorithms applicable and allows uncertainty-reducing plans without explicitly computing joint estimates during planning. The authors demonstrate the approach using a standard algorithm on active-perception problems and report improved scalability as the planning horizon grows. The result connects a difficult centralized evaluation objective to established decentralized planning machinery while accounting for the possible cost of that conversion.
neurips-2020-multi-agent-active-percepti.tldr: Individual prediction actions turn cooperative sensing with a centralized reward into standard decentralized planning, with bounded loss and improved empirical horizon scalability.

paragraphs: Dense Transformer attention connects every position in a sequence to every other position, producing a quadratic number of connections per layer. Sparse attention reduces those connections, making it attractive for long sequences. The paper asks whether this reduction also removes the ability to represent functions that dense Transformers can approximate.

The authors develop a unifying framework covering existing sparse attention models and identify sufficient conditions for universal approximation of sequence-to-sequence functions. Under those conditions, a sparse Transformer with only a linear number of attention connections per layer can approximate the same function class as a dense model with quadratically many connections.

This is a statement about representational capacity for qualifying sparse patterns. It does not assert that every way of removing attention connections preserves that capacity. The paper also compares sparsity patterns and levels in experiments on standard language tasks. Together, the theory and experiments address complementary questions: which sparse structures retain broad approximation power, and how choices of sparsity behave in evaluated tasks. The main theoretical finding shows that quadratic connectivity is not required for the stated approximation capability.
neurips-2020-o-n-connections-are-express.tldr: Under sufficient structural conditions, sparse Transformers with linear attention connections per layer retain the universal approximation capacity of dense models.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with function approximation must manage two difficulties together: deciding when to explore and estimating values from limited data. The paper seeks guarantees for both computation and sample use in episodic learning. It focuses on action-value functions represented by kernels or over-parameterized neural networks.

The proposed algorithm adds optimism to least-squares value iteration. For both representation settings, the authors establish polynomial runtime and sample complexity without additional assumptions on the data-generating model. They prove a regret bound proportional to the intrinsic complexity of the function class, the square of episode length, and the square root of the number of episodes, up to logarithmic factors.

A key feature of the bound is that it does not depend on the number of states, which may even diverge. The guarantee instead reflects the complexity of the chosen function representation. This explains the theoretical benefit of approximation in large state spaces: learning can be controlled through representational complexity rather than by counting states individually. The claim remains tied to the stated episodic kernel and over-parameterized neural settings.
neurips-2020-provably-efficient-reinforc.tldr: Optimistic least-squares value iteration achieves polynomial efficiency and state-count-independent regret guarantees with kernel or over-parameterized neural value representations.

paragraphs: Semantic segmentation assigns a category to each image pixel, and contextual information helps inform those assignments. RANet organizes this context around relationships between object regions. The approach divides an image into regions and selects representative information from each, giving the network regional content to exchange across the image.

The network configures pathways between pixels in different regions so that regional interactions can enrich pixel representations. Region construction, representative-content selection, pathway configuration, and context exchange are trained jointly. These components therefore form one learned segmentation system, with the regional organization and the use of its information optimized together.

The authors evaluate the method on challenging segmentation benchmarks and report that RANet helps achieve state-of-the-art results. The stated findings support region-level interaction as an effective way to build context for pixel-level prediction. The central contribution is the coordinated design: regions provide representative content, learned connections determine where that content travels, and exchanges between regions enhance information available to pixels. This connects object-region organization directly to the final task of assigning labels throughout an image.
neurips-2020-ranet-region-attention-netw.tldr: RANet jointly learns object regions and information exchange between them to improve pixel-level semantic segmentation.

paragraphs: Learning physical dynamics can benefit from representing a system through its Hamiltonian or Lagrangian rather than directly learning its differential equations. The paper examines a design choice within these physics-informed models: how to represent the system's coordinates and constraints. Earlier approaches encode constraints through generalized coordinates.

The authors instead embed the system in Cartesian coordinates and enforce constraints explicitly using Lagrange multipliers. They show that this formulation dramatically simplifies the learning problem. The choice concerns how physical structure enters the model: the coordinate representation and the enforcement of constraints become explicit parts of the learning setup.

The evaluation includes challenging chaotic and extended-body systems involving multiple pendulums, spring coupling, magnetic fields, rigid rotors, and gyroscopes. In these experiments, the authors report a 100-fold improvement in accuracy and data efficiency from using Cartesian coordinates with explicit constraints. These results make coordinate choice a substantive modeling consideration, showing that retaining Hamiltonian or Lagrangian structure while changing how constraints are expressed can substantially improve the evaluated learning problems.
neurips-2020-simplifying-hamiltonian-and.tldr: Using Cartesian coordinates with explicit constraints simplifies Hamiltonian and Lagrangian learning and yields reported 100-fold experimental gains in accuracy and data efficiency.

paragraphs: Modeling many categorical variables requires describing both the categories each variable takes and the relationships among variables. The full Potts model offers flexibility, but its parameter count becomes difficult to support when there are many categories. This paper introduces a smaller model intended to retain useful multivariate dependence structure.

The Potts-Ising model combines general categorical marginal distributions with Ising-type dependence. For d variables with K categories, it reduces the parameter count from at least order d squared times K squared to order d squared plus K times d. The reduction separates the category-related parameter burden from the much larger category-by-category interaction burden of the full Potts model.

The authors show that fitting the new model has the same complexity as fitting an Ising model. Using neighborhood regression, estimation reduces to d separate logistic regressions. Comparisons with existing approaches demonstrate that the model can capture multivariate dependencies. The contribution is a specific balance between categorical flexibility and structured dependence, making estimation substantially more compact while preserving the ability to model relationships among variables.
neurips-2020-the-potts-ising-model-for-d.tldr: The Potts-Ising model captures categorical dependencies with far fewer parameters than a full Potts model and can be fitted through separate logistic regressions.

paragraphs: Machine-learning compilers face several related decisions when turning computational graphs into efficient execution. Solving these decisions individually with heuristics can miss their dependencies. The paper introduces GO, a transferable deep reinforcement-learning approach that combines an inductive graph neural network with a scalable sequential attention mechanism.

GO makes decisions for an entire graph instead of selecting them one node at a time autoregressively, accelerating the search. Recurrent attention layers also allow it to optimize dependent graph tasks jointly. The architecture is designed to address both the cost of searching for decisions and the need to handle graphs not seen during learning.

Across three graph-optimization tasks, the authors report speedups of 33% to 60% over TensorFlow's default optimization. For device placement evaluated on real systems, graphs include up to 80,000 nodes and architectures such as Inception-v3, Transformer-XL, and WaveNet. On that task, GO reports average improvements of 21% over human experts and 18% over the previous state of the art, with 15 times faster convergence. These findings support learned, coordinated optimization on the evaluated compiler workloads.
neurips-2020-transferable-graph-optimize.tldr: GO uses transferable graph-based reinforcement learning to coordinate compiler decisions, accelerating search and improving reported execution performance.

paragraphs: Private stochastic gradient descent clips each example's gradient when its length exceeds a threshold. This is a key part of the training procedure, but clipping can distort the update direction. The paper first demonstrates that this distortion can prevent SGD from reaching a stationary point, making clipping bias a genuine optimization issue.

The authors then analyze that bias geometrically. They characterize its effect on the gradient norm and bound it using the Wasserstein distance between the gradient distribution and a geometrically symmetric distribution. This relates the potential harm from clipping to the shape of the gradients encountered during training.

Their experiments suggest that gradient distributions along private-SGD training trajectories do exhibit the relevant symmetry. Combined with the theory, this offers an explanation for why clipping can work well in practice despite its possible bias; the empirical symmetry is evidence, not a universal property of training. The authors also propose a perturbation-based technique that provably corrects clipping bias even for highly asymmetric gradient distributions. The paper therefore supplies both an account of practical effectiveness and a method for addressing problematic asymmetry.
neurips-2020-understanding-gradient-clip.tldr: A geometric analysis links private-SGD clipping bias to gradient asymmetry and motivates a provable perturbation-based correction.
